steps.title: Right fix: latest row per key, then MERGE
steps.plain: Silver keeps one row per business key (order_id): the most recent event, by ingestion time. MERGE on order_id writes it, so a retried batch, a duplicate event or a re-run changes nothing. Ran the MERGE twice on purpose: still 4 rows and ₹2,790. Order 1003 shows its latest status, paid.

w = Window.partitionBy('order_id').orderBy(desc('_ingested_at'), desc('event_id'))
latest = bronze.withColumn('_rn', row_number().over(w)).filter('_rn = 1')

MERGE INTO dupes.silver_ok t USING latest s ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s._ingested_at > t._ingested_at THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
-- run twice: same result

steps.title: Right fix: rebuild the history of affected keys, in source order
steps.plain: For every customer touched by the batch, take all of their changes ever (old and new), order them by when they happened in the source (changed_at, never load time), drop changes that change nothing (hash equals the previous one), and derive valid_to from the next version. Then replace just those customers' rows in one atomic write (replaceWhere). Ran twice. Asha: Pune → Goa (20 Oct) → Mumbai → Sydney, current = Sydney; on 25 Oct she lived in Goa. Ravi: still one version.
steps.code:
WITH affected AS (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM batch),
     ordered AS (
       SELECT c.*, sha2(concat_ws('|', city, email), 256) AS h,
              lag(sha2(concat_ws('|', city, email), 256)) OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) AS prev_h
       FROM scd.changes c JOIN affected USING (customer_id)),
     versions AS (SELECT * FROM ordered WHERE prev_h IS NULL OR h <> prev_h)      -- drop no-op changes
SELECT customer_id, city, email, changed_at AS valid_from,
       lead(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) AS valid_to,
       lead(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) IS NULL AS is_current
FROM versions

# replace only the affected customers, atomically
hist.write.format('delta').mode('overwrite').option('replaceWhere', "customer_id IN ('C-77','C-80')").saveAsTable('scd.silver')

steps.title: Right fix: every step safe to repeat, plus a run log
steps.plain: Each step is idempotent (MERGE into silver, replace the day in gold) and records itself in a run log. After the crash, the re-run skips silver (already done) and builds gold. steps.title: Right fix: a contract check before the write, and a mapping in the manifest
steps.plain: Before writing, the job compares what arrived with the contract. A missing required column (amount) is a breaking change: the load stops, nothing is written (the table stayed at version 0), and the source owner is alerted. A new column (coupon) is additive, so it is allowed to evolve. The fix is one line in the manifest, renames: order_amount → amount, reviewed as a PR. The re-run passes the check and lands 27 Oct correctly: ₹1,990.

required: [order_id, amount, placed_at]
on_missing_required: stop_and_alert
on_new_column: evolve        # additive changes are safe
renames: {order_amount: amount}   # added by PR after the alert

missing, new = contract_check(incoming)
if missing: stop_and_alert(missing)   # breaking: nothing written
incoming = apply_renames(incoming)
write(incoming, mergeSchema=True)

steps.title: Right fix: incremental for changes, key reconciliation for deletes
steps.plain: Keep the cheap incremental load for changes. Add a second step: read only the keys from the source (one narrow column) and MERGE with WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE. Any active key in silver that the source no longer has is soft-deleted: is_deleted = true, with the date. Run 1 marked 1 row; run 2 marked 0, so it is safe to repeat. C-0003 stays in silver for history and old orders, and drops out of every 'active' view. If the source can publish change data capture (CDC) with delete events, use those instead; this reconciliation is the safety net.
steps.code:
MERGE INTO silver t
USING (SELECT * FROM dels.src WHERE updated_at > timestamp'2026-10-20 08:00:00') s     -- only rows changed since the last run
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET city = s.city, updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (customer_id, city, updated_at, is_deleted) VALUES (s.customer_id, s.city, s.updated_at, false)

-- then, the delete detector
MERGE INTO silver t
USING (SELECT customer_id FROM source.customers) s        -- keys only: one narrow column
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND NOT t.is_deleted
  THEN UPDATE SET is_deleted = true, deleted_at = timestamp'2026-10-27 23:00:00'

steps.title: Naive fix: patch gold by hand, in production
steps.plain: Someone compares 21 Oct with the source, works out that gold is short by a factor of 1.7424, and scales all five days by it with one UPDATE in production. 21 Oct now matches. The other days are close but not right, because each day had a different share of 'PAID' orders: revenue matches on 23 of 27 days. Order counts are still wrong, silver still lacks 20 orders, and gold now disagrees with silver on 5 days. Nobody can re-run this patch, and the next rebuild of gold will undo it.

steps.title: Right fix: a backfill command that re-runs the fixed job for a date range
steps.plain: The daily job takes the date as a parameter and replaces exactly that day in silver and gold (replaceWhere), so a backfill is just the same job in a loop: backfill('2026-10-21', '2026-10-25'). It reads bronze, which kept every raw row, so nothing has to be fetched from the source again. The hand patch is overwritten too. Ran twice: all 27 days match, and the other 22 days were never touched. On a real platform you run it in dev first; if bronze itself were wrong, you would replay from the landing files.
steps.code:
def run_day(d):            # the same job that runs every night
    silver_rows(d).write.mode('overwrite').option('replaceWhere', f"order_date = '{d}'").saveAsTable('silver')
    gold_rows(d).write.mode('overwrite').option('replaceWhere', f"order_date = '{d}'").saveAsTable('gold.daily')

def backfill(start, end):
    for d in dates(start, end):
        run_day(d)

backfill('2026-10-21', '2026-10-25')   # run twice: same result

steps.title: What you see: the same query, twice as slow and getting worse
steps.plain: Orders arrive every few minutes, and each small write adds one file per task (4 tasks): 150 writes of 200 orders made 600 files for 30,000 rows. The same rows in 1 file answer the dashboard query in 262 ms; this table takes 563 ms, 2.1× slower. Every file has to be listed, opened and read, and its footer parsed, however little data it holds. The table is tiny here, so the gap is in milliseconds; on a real lake with millions of files it grows to minutes.

steps.title: Naive fix: partition the table more finely
steps.plain: 'Partition it so queries only read what they need.' Partitioning by store splits every small write into one file per store per task: the same 150 writes now make 4,200 files, and the query that reads every store takes 2163 ms. Partitioning helps only when partitions are big (a common rule of thumb is about 1 GB each) and queries filter on them. Here it multiplied the problem. A bigger cluster only pays for the overhead; the files are still there.

steps.title: Right fix: compact the files (OPTIMIZE) and write bigger batches
steps.plain: OPTIMIZE rewrites many small files into a few large ones in a single commit: 600 files became 1, in 3560 ms. The data is identical; readers never see a half-compacted table, and old versions still work until VACUUM. The query now takes 325 ms, down from 563 ms (1.7× faster), against 262 ms for the one-file table. Run it on a schedule (or turn on auto-compaction on Databricks), and write fewer, bigger batches where the business allows.
steps.code:
OPTIMIZE orders            -- bin-pack small files into large ones, one atomic commit

SELECT store, count(*) AS orders, sum(amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY store ORDER BY store   -- median of 7 runs
